Solar Panel Power Meter

An Arduino-based instrument for measuring solar panel voltage, current, and power.

Project Overview

The Brief

For the EEE 202 Circuits I Lab final project, our team built a portable power meter for the Sparky Solar client scenario. The goal was to help field technicians check a small solar panel without calculating voltage, current, and power by hand. Affordability, readily available components, compact size, and operation at elevated temperatures guided the design.

The Prototype

We combined a voltage divider, a shunt resistor with a non-inverting amplifier, and an Arduino Uno. The Arduino reconstructs the panel voltage and load current from two analog inputs, calculates power, and refreshes an LCD once per second. Lab 7 documents development from individual sensing stages through controller tests and LCD integration, followed by a prototype demonstration signed off on May 1, 2026.

Signal Chain & Circuit Design

01 · Voltage Sensing

A 47 kΩ / 100 kΩ divider scales the panel voltage for analog input A1. At the measured 6.83 V maximum, the calculated divider output is about 4.64 V, below the Arduino's 5 V input limit.

Vout = Vin × 100 / (47 + 100)

02 · Current Sensing

A 50 Ω shunt in series with the 1 kΩ load converts current into a small voltage. A rail-to-rail, non-inverting op-amp with 22 kΩ input and 100 kΩ feedback resistors amplifies that signal before it reaches A0. The worksheet checks headroom at the load resistor's calculated 15.8 mA power limit: about 0.791 V across the shunt and 4.38 V after amplification.

Gain = 1 + 100 / 22 ≈ 5.55

03 · Processing & Display

The Arduino reverses the divider and amplifier scaling to recover voltage and current, then multiplies the values to calculate power. A diode prevents reverse current, and the LCD updates every second.

I = Vshunt / 50 Ω; P = V × I

Design Tradeoffs

  • Selected resistor set 2 for both sensing stages. The worksheet ranks divider priorities as availability, cost, then size; amplifier priorities are temperature rating, availability, then cost.
  • Chose high divider resistances to reduce power consumption, accepting greater sensitivity to noise and leakage.
  • Balanced current sensitivity and signal headroom with a nominal op-amp gain of 5.55; the calculated full-sun output was approximately 1.87 V.
  • Used a benchtop DC supply for steady indoor debugging before testing under changing outdoor light.

From ADC Readings to Engineering Units

Lab 7 explains how raw ADC readings become engineering units. Using the worksheet's nominal 5 V reference, a 1024-count conversion, and the selected resistor values:

Panel voltage (V)

Vpanel = ADC_A1 × (Vref / 1024) × (147 / 100)

Load current (mA)

Iload = ADC_A0 × (Vref / 1024) × 1000 / (5.545 × 50)

Power (mW)

P = Vpanel × Iload_mA

The worksheet uses Vref = 5.00 V. The final report describes replacing that nominal value with a measured 4.97 V during calibration.

Capacitor Discharge Analysis

Part 5 extends the project to first-order transient analysis. With the worksheet's equivalent resistance of 1 kΩ + 50 Ω = 1050 Ω, we solved for a capacitor that would discharge from 6 V to 1 mV in approximately 10 ms.

Vc(t) = V0 × exp(−t / (R × C))

C = −0.010 / (1050 × ln(0.001 / 6)) ≈ 1.1 µF

The worksheet documents the calculation. It does not include an oscilloscope discharge trace or a signed measurement for this optional test.

Simulation & Bench Development

Troubleshooting & Iteration

Correcting the ADC Reference

In full sun, the serial monitor showed 6.71 V while the handheld meter read 6.83 V. The conversion code assumed an exact 5.00 V reference.

We measured the Arduino's actual 5 V rail at 4.97 V and updated the conversion constant. The report records a subsequent voltage error below 0.2%.

Establishing a Common Ground

During assembly, the LCD flickered and the readings jumped. Checking the power rails and tracing signals with an oscilloscope revealed that the op-amp stage and Arduino lacked a shared ground.

A jumper between the op-amp ground rail and Arduino GND stabilized the readings. This highlighted the importance of a consistent reference across analog and digital stages.

The initial lighting survey, individual circuit tests, and integrated LCD tests are separate measurements. The worksheet's full-sun LCD voltage differs from the final report's calibration result; neither establishes accuracy across the full voltage and current range.

Lessons & Next Steps

This build connected circuit theory to physical measurement: resistor tolerances, amplifier offset, the ADC reference, and breadboard wiring all affected the result. Comparing simulation, hand calculations, and bench readings helped us locate errors systematically instead of replacing components at random.

Beyond the Breadboard

The demonstrated result is a small-panel breadboard prototype. Next steps would include checking voltage and current calibration at multiple points, repeating tests under controlled inputs, and measuring the calculated capacitor discharge response. A field-ready version would also need a weather-resistant enclosure, corrosion-resistant terminals, and thermal validation. Larger installations would require a redesigned sensing and protection system and potentially data logging or remote readout.
